### 7.3 Proof of Proposition 7.1

With the two ingredients established above, the limiting BAR can now be closed: Lemma 7.1 controls the boundary and non-basic-activity terms, while Lemma 7.2 converts the remaining activity-specific service terms into the transform $\phi^{(r)}(\theta)$ .

#### Proof.

Applying Lemma 4.1 to $f_{\theta}(z)$ defined in $(\ref{eq:ef})$ and using a second-order Taylor expansion, with $0\leq f_{\theta}({z})\leq 1$ , we obtain the following BAR after dividing both sides by $r\theta$ :

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}\phi_{k}^{(r)}(\theta)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}d_{ik}\phi_{ik}^{(r)}(\theta)-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}r\phi^{(r)}(\theta) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v^{2}_{i}r\theta\phi^{(r)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}u_{k}v_{i}r\theta\phi_{ik}^{(r)}(\theta)+O(r^{2})=0. $$

Applying Lemma 7.1, the BAR becomes

$$ \displaystyle r+O(r^{3/2})-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}r\phi^{(r)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v^{2}_{i}r\theta\phi^{(r)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}u_{k}v_{i}r\theta\phi_{ik}^{(r)}(\theta)=0. $$

Using $\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}=1$ in Lemma 3.1, and rearranging some terms, the BAR implies

$$ \displaystyle r-r\phi^{(r)}(\theta)+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v^{2}_{i}r\theta\phi^{(r)}(\theta)+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{I}v_{i}r\theta\left(\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}u_{k}\phi^{(r)}_{ik}(\theta)-\lambda_{i}v_{i}\phi^{(r)}(\theta)\right)=O(r^{3/2}). $$

Dividing both sides by $r$ and then applying Lemma 7.2, the last term converges to zero as $r\downarrow 0$ . Hence,

$$ \displaystyle(1-\theta\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v^{2}_{i})\lim_{r\downarrow 0}\phi^{(r)}(\theta)=1. $$

This completes the proof of Proposition 7.1. ∎

### 7.4 Proof of Theorem 3.1

#### Proof.

Denote

$$ U^{(r)}\triangleq r\bigg(\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}W_{k}({Z}^{(r)})\bigg)=r\bigg(\sum_{k=1}^{K}u^{2}_{k}T_{k}({Z}^{(r)})\bigg). $$

Let $e=(1,\ldots,1)^{\top}$ . Corollary 7.1 can then be written in vector form as

$$ {}U^{(r)}e\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\tilde{X}e,\quad\text{as }r\downarrow 0. $$

Now denote $Y^{(r)}=(Y_{1}^{(r)},\ldots,Y_{K}^{(r)})^{\top}$ , where

$$ Y_{k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\triangleq r\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}\right)\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime}}({Z}^{(r)})=r\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}T_{k^{\prime}}({Z}^{(r)}),\quad k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}. $$

Taking the difference, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Big\|U^{(r)}e-Y^{(r)}\Big\|\leq\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}\left|U^{(r)}-Y_{k^{\prime}}^{(r)}\right|\leq\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}r\left[\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}\left|T_{k}({Z}^{(r)})-T_{k^{\prime}}({Z}^{(r)})\right|\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{k^{\prime}=1}^{K}r\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}\left(T_{(K)}({Z}^{(r)})-T_{(1)}({Z}^{(r)})\right)\leq rK\left(T_{(K)}({Z}^{(r)})-T_{(1)}({Z}^{(r)})\right), $$

where the last inequality uses $\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}\leq 1$ . By Proposition 5.1 and Markov’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\left\|U^{(r)}e-Y^{(r)}\right\|\stackrel{{\scriptstyle p}}{{\rightarrow}}0,\quad\text{as }r\downarrow 0. $$

Combining (7.32) and (7.33) and applying Theorem 3.1 of Billingsley (1999), we obtain

$$ Y^{(r)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\tilde{X}e,\quad\text{as }r\downarrow 0, $$

i.e.,

$$ r\left(\sum_{k=1}^{K}u^{2}_{k}\right)\left(\frac{1}{u_{1}}W_{1}({Z}^{(r)}),\ldots,\frac{1}{u_{K}}W_{K}({Z}^{(r)})\right)^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\tilde{X}e, $$

where, recall, $\tilde{X}$ is an exponential random variable with mean $m=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}^{2}$ . Then, by the scaling property of the exponential distribution, we have

$$ \displaystyle r\left(W_{1}({Z}^{(r)}),\ldots,W_{K}({Z}^{(r)})\right)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{\rightarrow}}\left(u_{1},\ldots,u_{K}\right)X,\quad\text{as }r\downarrow 0, $$

where $X$ is an exponential random variable with mean

$$ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}^{2}}{\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{2}}. $$

∎

## 8 Further Discussion

### 8.1 A Comparison of Routing and Scheduling Policies

Under the OQ architecture, we need to specify a routing policy and a scheduling policy, while under the IQ architecture, only a scheduling policy is needed. In this section, we use an X-model example to explore how routing and scheduling policies affect stability under different architectures. Figures 3 and 3 show the X model under the OQ and IQ architectures, respectively. We set the same parameters for both as

$$ \lambda_{1}=1.3\rho,\quad\lambda_{2}=0.4\rho,\quad\mu_{1}=\mu_{3}=\mu_{4}=1,\quad\mu_{2}=0.5,\quad\rho=0.95. $$

Under this parameter setting, solving the associated static allocation problem shows that activity $(2,1)$ is non-basic, as indicated by the dashed edges in Figures 3 and 3. For the OQ X-model, we compare JSQ and WWTA routing, both combined with the priority scheduling rule. For the IQ X-model, we compare the priority rule with MaxWeight scheduling. For priority scheduling, we use a preemptive shortest-mean-processing-first static buffer priority rule, with ties broken in favor of class 2; in this example, class 2 jobs therefore have preemptive priority over class 1 jobs whenever both are available. Each policy setting is simulated at 95% system load (i.e., $\rho=0.95$ ). Figure 4(a) shows the total number of jobs in the system over time, and Figure 4(b) provides a zoomed-in comparison of the two stable policies, WWTA with priority scheduling under OQ and MaxWeight under IQ.

As shown in Figure 4(a), JSQ with priority scheduling under the OQ architecture is unstable, while WWTA with the same priority scheduling is stable. This shows that using queue lengths alone for routing may not be sufficient in systems with heterogeneous job classes and server types: even when the overall system load is below capacity, JSQ does not distinguish between slow and fast activities and may route too many jobs through slow activities. Under the IQ architecture, priority scheduling is unstable, whereas MaxWeight scheduling is stable. This indicates that, in IQ systems, the choice of scheduling policy can be critical for stability, as an intuitive priority rule may not suffice.

Taken together, these comparisons illustrate how the load-balancing role is handled differently across the two architectures: under IQ, jobs wait in class queues and load balancing is maintained through scheduling decisions, whereas under OQ with immediate job assignment, routing decisions play the critical role in balancing the load, leaving the choice of scheduling policy as an additional degree of freedom. In particular, WWTA with the priority scheduling rule is stable in the OQ X-model, whereas the same scheduling rule is unstable in the IQ X-model.

### 8.2 Service Policies and Scheduling Flexibility

In OQ systems, a scheduling policy determines how each server allocates its service effort to different job classes. In this section, we introduce several scheduling rules that can be used as local service policies while WWTA handles load balancing through routing. We use a W-model example to demonstrate that, although the choice of scheduling policy does not affect the theoretical results established in the paper, it may affect other performance measures, such as delay.

We consider two types of service policies that can be implemented with WWTA. The first type of service policy is the head-of-line proportional processor sharing (HLPPS) scheduling policy (Bramson, 1998). Under HLPPS, all nonempty buffers receive service simultaneously. For each server $k\in\mathcal{K}$ , the proportion of effort that server $k$ allocates among classes $\mathcal{I}(k)$ at any time is given by

$$ \displaystyle P_{ik}(z)=\frac{z_{ik}}{\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{I}(k)}z_{i^{\prime}k}},\quad i\in\mathcal{I}(k), $$

when the state is $z=(z_{ik})$ . Here, we adopt the convention that ${0}/{0}=0$ , which means that when $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}z_{ik}=0$ , server $k$ is idle. Therefore, the instantaneous service rate for activity $j=(i,k)$ is $\mu_{ik}P_{ik}(z)$ . The implementation of the HLPPS policy does not require knowledge of system parameters, such as arrival rates or service rates. It also does not depend on the routing policy, but only on the relative queue sizes of the buffers at each server.

The allocation in (8.34) can also be generalized to

$$ P_{ik}({z})=\frac{c_{ik}z_{ik}}{\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{I}(k)}c_{i^{\prime}k}z_{i^{\prime}k}},\quad i\in\mathcal{I}(k),k\in\mathcal{K}, $$

where $c=(c_{ik})>0$ is a given vector of positive numbers. We call the service policy using allocation (8.35) a generalized HLPPS policy with weights $c=(c_{ik})$ .

The second type of service policy is the static buffer priority (SBP) scheduling policy. Each SBP policy specifies a fixed ranking of the buffers at each server. Given a ranking, we write $(i^{\prime},k)\prec(i,k)$ to denote that buffer $(i^{\prime},k)$ has preemptive priority over buffer $(i,k)$ . Formally, we can define the SBP service policy for server $k$ in terms of $P_{ik}(z)$ values as follows

$$ P_{ik}({z})=\mathbbm{1}\Big(\sum_{(i^{\prime},k)\prec(i,k)}z_{i^{\prime}k}=0,z_{ik}>0\Big). $$

*Figure 5: W model under the OQ architecture.*

We next examine how the choice of scheduling policy affects delay performance. We use a W model with three job classes and two servers, where the name “W” comes from its W-shaped structure. The W model provides a richer setting for illustrating the impact of local scheduling decisions than the X model considered above. Figure 5 depicts the W model under the OQ architecture. We set

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{1}=4\rho,\quad\lambda_{2}=1.3\rho,\quad\lambda_{3}=0.4\rho,\quad\mu_{11}=8,\quad\mu_{21}=2,\quad\mu_{31}=0.25, \displaystyle\mu_{12}=0.25,\quad\mu_{22}=0.5,\quad\mu_{32}=1,\quad\rho\in(0,1). $$

We implement WWTA with each of the two service policies introduced above: HLPPS and the shortest-mean-processing-first SBP rule. As a reference, we also implement MaxWeight scheduling under the corresponding IQ architecture, where jobs wait in class-specific queues, as in the IQ X-model shown in Figure 3. Under these system parameters, activities $(3,1)$ and $(1,2)$ are non-basic. Our performance metric is the average of the class-specific mean completion times, where the completion time of a job is measured from its arrival to its service completion and departure.

We conduct the simulations at eight system load levels $\rho$ ranging from $92\%$ to $99\%$ . For each combination of load level and policy, we perform 30 independent replications of a discrete-event simulation, each run for 50,000 time units starting from an empty system, to obtain $95\%$ confidence intervals for this performance metric. As shown in Figure 6, the two WWTA implementations exhibit different delay performance, with SBP consistently yielding shorter average completion times than HLPPS. WWTA with either HLPPS or SBP scheduling yields shorter average completion times than MaxWeight over the range of loads considered. The performance differences become more pronounced as the system approaches heavy traffic.

*Figure 6: Average of the class-specific mean completion times in the W model.*

Taken together, these results illustrate that the scheduling flexibility enabled by WWTA can have a substantial impact on delay performance, with local service policies potentially tailored even on a server-by-server basis. This suggests an interesting direction for future work: optimizing local service policies for delay, cost, or value objectives, while leaving system-level load balancing and the handling of non-basic activities to WWTA routing.

## Appendix A Proofs in Section 3 and Section 4

### A.1 Proof of Lemma 3.1

#### Proof.

Under Assumption 3.1, strong duality implies that the dual LP has an optimal solution $({v}^{*},{u}^{*})$ with zero duality gap. Therefore,

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v^{*}_{i}=\rho^{*}=1. $$

Since $\rho^{*}=1$ , complementary slackness for the primal variable $\rho$ gives

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{K}u^{*}_{k}=1. $$

Moreover, $u^{*}_{k}\geq 0$ follows from dual feasibility. For each activity $j=(i,k)$ , complementary slackness also gives

$$ x_{j}^{*}\big[(u^{*}A)_{j}-(v^{*}R)_{j}\big]=0. $$

Hence, if $x_{ik}^{*}>0$ , then $(v^{*}R)_{j}=(u^{*}A)_{j}$ . Since $(v^{*}R)_{j}=\mu_{ik}v_{i}^{*}$ and $(u^{*}A)_{j}=u_{k}^{*}$ , we obtain

$$ \mu_{ik}v_{i}^{*}=u_{k}^{*}. $$

∎

### A.2 Proof of Lemma 3.2

#### Proof.

Starting with any server $k$ , denote $u_{k}^{*}=a\geq 0$ . By Assumption 3.2, server $k$ is connected to all other servers through chains of basic activities. As an illustration, suppose that server $k$ has two communicating servers $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ , which communicate directly with server $k$ through classes $i_{1}$ and $i_{2}$ , respectively:

$$ \displaystyle\text{server }k \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{class }i_{1}}}{{\longrightarrow}} \displaystyle\text{server }k_{1} \displaystyle\downarrow_{\text{class }i_{2}} \displaystyle\text{server }k_{2} $$

In other words, server $k$ communicates with $k_{1}$ through the basic activities $(i_{1},k)$ and $(i_{1},k_{1})$ , and with $k_{2}$ through the basic activities $(i_{2},k)$ and $(i_{2},k_{2})$ .

For any optimal primal solution $x^{*}$ and any optimal dual solution $(v^{*},u^{*})$ , complementary slackness gives $\mu_{ik}v_{i}^{*}=u_{k}^{*}$ whenever $x_{ik}^{*}>0$ . Hence, this equality holds along all basic activities used to establish communication, even if they correspond to different optimal primal solutions. Thus, we can write

$$ v^{*}_{i_{1}}=\frac{u^{*}_{k}}{\mu_{i_{1}{k}}}=\frac{a}{\mu_{i_{1}{k}}},\quad v^{*}_{i_{2}}=\frac{u^{*}_{k}}{\mu_{i_{2}{k}}}=\frac{a}{\mu_{i_{2}{k}}}; $$

$$ \displaystyle u^{*}_{k_{1}}=v^{*}_{i_{1}}\mu_{i_{1}k_{1}}=a\frac{\mu_{i_{1}k_{1}}}{\mu_{i_{1}{k}}},\quad u^{*}_{k_{2}}=v^{*}_{i_{2}}\mu_{i_{2}k_{2}}=a\frac{\mu_{i_{2}k_{2}}}{\mu_{i_{2}{k}}}. $$

Thus, $u_{k_{1}}^{*}$ and $u_{k_{2}}^{*}$ can be expressed as $a$ multiplied by ratios of service rates.

Similarly, starting with servers $k_{1}$ and $k_{2}$ , we can find other communicating servers through basic activities and obtain $u_{k_{3}}^{*},u_{k_{4}}^{*},\ldots$ , each expressed as $a$ multiplied by ratios of service rates. Continuing this procedure, Assumption 3.2 guarantees that we can eventually reach all servers and obtain such an expression for each server. Finally, by Lemma 3.1(ii), $\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{*}=1$ , which uniquely determines $a$ . Tracing back through these equations then uniquely determines each component of $(v^{*},u^{*})$ .

In the discussion above, at each step we select one class through which two servers communicate. This choice need not be unique, and some equalities corresponding to other basic activities may therefore not be used in determining $(v^{*},u^{*})$ . However, the choice of communication paths does not affect uniqueness. Once the selected communication paths and the normalization $\sum_{k}u_{k}^{*}=1$ uniquely determine $(v^{*},u^{*})$ , the unused equalities impose only additional constraints that this unique optimal dual solution must satisfy.

For Lemma 3.2(ii), since $u_{k}^{*}\geq 0$ for all $k$ and $\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}^{*}=1$ , there exists at least one server $k$ with $u_{k}^{*}>0$ . Starting from this server and applying the same equations as above, we obtain $u_{k}^{*}>0$ for all $k\in\mathcal{K}$ . Since each class has at least one basic activity and $\mu_{ik}>0$ , the relation $\mu_{ik}v_{i}^{*}=u_{k}^{*}$ then implies $v_{i}^{*}>0$ for all $i\in\mathcal{I}$ . ∎

### A.3 Proof of Lemma 4.1

#### Proof.

Assume $f:\mathbb{Z}^{J}_{+}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $|f({z})|\leq C\big(1+\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\big)$ for some $C>0$ . Following Braverman et al. (2016), we use the following sufficient condition given in Henderson (1997); Glynn and Zeevi (2008) for $\mathbb{E}\left[Gf\left({Z}^{(r)}\right)\right]=0$ :

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[\left|G\left({Z}^{(r)},{Z}^{(r)}\right)f\big({Z}^{(r)}\big)\right|\right]<\infty, $$

where $G({z},{z})$ is the diagonal element of the generator matrix $G$ corresponding to state ${z}$ . First, we have

$$ \displaystyle\left|G\left({Z}^{(r)},{Z}^{(r)}\right)\right| \displaystyle= \displaystyle\bigg|-\bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}^{(r)}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}{(i)}}\mathbbm{1}\left(k=L^{(i)}({Z}^{(r)})\right)+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\mu_{ik}P_{ik}\left({Z}^{(r)}\right)\bigg)\bigg| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\mu_{ik}. $$

Therefore, by the assumed bound on $f$ , it suffices to show that $\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\Big[W_{k}^{n}\Big(Z^{(r)}\Big)\Big]<\infty$ . Define

$$ V({z})=\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n+1}_{k}(z). $$

The generator of $V$ can be written in terms of the binomial expansion as follows:

$$ \displaystyle GV({z})= \displaystyle\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}^{(r)}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{n+1}{n+1\choose\ell}m_{ik}^{\ell}W_{k}^{n+1-\ell}(z)\right)\mathbbm{1}\left(k=L^{(i)}(z)\right) \displaystyle+\frac{1}{n+1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\frac{\mu_{ik}P_{ik}(z)}{u_{k}^{n-1}}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{n+1}{n+1\choose\ell}\left(-m_{ik}\right)^{\ell}W_{k}^{n+1-\ell}(z)\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}^{(r)}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{m_{ik}}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\left(k=L^{(i)}(z)\right) \displaystyle-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}P_{ik}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\leq}} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}^{(r)}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{v_{i}^{n-1}}\left(m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\right)^{n}\mathbbm{1}\left(k=L^{(i)}(z)\right)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{=}} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{\lambda_{i}^{(r)}}{v_{i}^{n-1}}\min_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\left(m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\right)^{n}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big), $$

where the terms of lower order are written as $o\big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}^{n}(z)\big)$ as $\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}^{n}(z)\to\infty$ . $(a)$ follows from (4.8) and the non-idling property of $\mathcal{P}$ , and $(b)$ follows from the definition of the WWTA policy. Under Assumption 3.1, we choose an optimal processing plan $x^{*}$ and define $\lambda_{ik}\triangleq x^{*}_{ik}\mu_{ik}$ for $(i,k)\in\mathcal{J}$ . Then $\lambda_{ik}$ satisfies $\lambda_{i}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}$ and $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\lambda_{ik}m_{ik}=1$ . Let $\lambda^{(r)}_{ik}=\lambda_{ik}(1-r)$ . Then $\lambda_{i}^{(r)}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}$ and $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}m_{ik}=1-r<1$ . Following an argument similar to that in the proof of Theorem 11.6 of Dai and Harrison (2020), we have

$$ \displaystyle GV({z})\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{1}{v_{i}^{n-1}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}\left(\frac{1}{\mu_{ik}}W_{k}(z)\right)^{n}-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{=}} \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{nb}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\frac{1}{(u_{k}-d_{ik})^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z) \displaystyle-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{nb}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\frac{1}{(u_{k}-d_{ik})^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z)-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{nb}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}W^{n}_{k}(z) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}-1\right)W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle+\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{nb}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}\left(\frac{1}{(u_{k}-d_{ik})^{n-1}}-\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}\right)W^{n}_{k}(z), $$

where $(c)$ follows by considering basic and non-basic activities separately and applying (4.8). The last term is zero because, for each activity with $d_{ik}>0$ , complementary slackness gives $x_{ik}^{*}=0$ , and hence $\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}=0$ . Therefore, the generator becomes

$$ \displaystyle GV({z})= \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{1}{u_{k}^{n-1}}\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\frac{\lambda_{ik}^{(r)}}{\mu_{ik}}-1\right)W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle-\frac{r}{\bar{u}^{n-1}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big), $$

where $\bar{u}\triangleq\max_{k\in\mathcal{K}}u_{k}>0$ . Therefore, there exist constants $c>0$ and $c_{w}>0$ such that, whenever $\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\geq c_{w}$ ,

$$ -\frac{r}{\bar{u}^{n-1}}\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)+o\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)\Big)\leq-cr\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z). $$

Consequently, there exists $d>0$ such that

$$ GV({z})\leq-cr\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)+d\mathbbm{1}\bigg(\sum_{k=1}^{K}W^{n}_{k}(z)<c_{w}\bigg). $$

By Theorem 4.3 of Meyn and Tweedie (1993), we have

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{E}\bigg[W_{k}^{n}\Big(Z^{(r)}\Big)\bigg]<\infty. $$

∎

## Appendix B Proofs in Section 5

### B.1 Proof of Lemma 5.1

Before proving Lemma 5.1, we first present the following lemma.

#### Lemma B.1.

For any $p,x\in\mathbb{R}$ with $p>0$ and $x\geq-1$ , the following inequality holds:

$$ \frac{x}{(1+x)^{p}+1}\leq\frac{x}{2}. $$

#### Proof of Lemma B.1.

If $x=0$ , equality holds. If $x>0$ , then $(1+x)^{p}+1>2$ . If $-1\leq x<0$ , then $(1+x)^{p}+1<2$ . Therefore, the inequality holds for all $x\geq-1$ . ∎

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

When a class $i$ job is routed to server $k$ , the incremental change in the perpendicular component $W_{\perp}(z)$ is

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{ik} \displaystyle=W(z)+m_{ik}e^{(k)}-\big[W_{\parallel}(z)+\langle m_{ik}e^{(k)},\hat{u}\rangle\hat{u}\big]-[W(z)-W_{\parallel}(z)] \displaystyle=m_{ik}e^{(k)}-\langle m_{ik}e^{(k)},\hat{u}\rangle\hat{u}. $$

Furthermore, since $\hat{u}^{\top}W_{\perp}(z)=0$ ,

$$ \delta_{ik}^{\top}W_{\perp}(z)=m_{ik}e^{(k)\top}W_{\perp}(z)=m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z), $$

where $W_{\perp,k}(z)$ denotes the $k$ th element of the vector $W_{\perp}(z)$ . A similar observation applies to a service completion at server $k$ for a class $i$ job.

We first assume $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|\geq 1$ and treat the case $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|<1$ at the end of the proof. With the test function (5.14) and incremental change (B.36), we write

$$ \displaystyle f(z+e_{ik})-f(z)= \displaystyle\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{n+1}-\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{2(n+1)}-\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2(n+1)}}{\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{n+1}+\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}}. $$

Using (B.37) and the binomial expansion, the numerator can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{2(n+1)}=\bigg[\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}+2\delta_{ik}^{\top}W_{\perp}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\bigg]^{n+1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2(n+1)}+(n+1)\bigg[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\bigg]\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2n}+A_{1}(z), $$

where $A_{1}(z)\triangleq\sum_{\ell=2}^{n+1}{n+1\choose\ell}\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]^{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2(n+1-\ell)}.$ Substituting this into (B.38), one has

$$ f(z+e_{ik})-f(z)=\frac{(n+1)\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2n}}{\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{n+1}+\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}}+\frac{A_{1}(z)}{\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{n+1}+\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}}. $$

For the first term in (B.39), dividing both the numerator and denominator by $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\frac{(n+1)\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n-1}}{\big[1+\frac{2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}}{\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}}\big]^{\frac{n+1}{2}}+1} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\frac{(n+1)\frac{\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]}{\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}}{\big[1+\frac{2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}}{\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}}\big]^{\frac{n+1}{2}}+1} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle(n+1)\frac{\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]}{2\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}, $$

where the second equality rearranges the expression into the form of Lemma B.1, which yields the last inequality. For the second term, note that

$$ \displaystyle\frac{A_{1}(z)}{\|W_{\perp}(z)+\delta_{ik}\|^{n+1}+\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}}\leq\frac{\sum_{\ell=2}^{n+1}{n+1\choose\ell}\big[2m_{ik}\big|W_{\perp,k}(z)\big|+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]^{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2(n+1-\ell)}}{\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}} \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{\ell=2}^{n+1}{n+1\choose\ell}\big[2m_{ik}\big\|W_{\perp}(z)\big\|+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]^{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1-2\ell}\triangleq\sum_{\ell=-(n+1)}^{n-1}\tilde{c}_{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{\ell}\leq\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}c^{\prime}_{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{\ell}, $$

where the equality marked by $\triangleq$ follows by expanding the powers and collecting terms according to the powers of $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|$ , with $\tilde{c}_{\ell}>0$ denoting the resulting constants. For the last inequality, since $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|\geq 1$ , the negative-power terms can be absorbed into the constant term, yielding some constants $c^{\prime}_{\ell}>0$ , $\ell=0,\ldots,n-1$ . Therefore, $(\ref{eq:ssc2})$ becomes

$$ \displaystyle f(z+e_{ik})-f(z)\leq \displaystyle(n+1)\frac{\big[2m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)+\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}\big]}{2\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{2}}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n+1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}c^{\prime}_{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{\ell} \displaystyle= \displaystyle(n+1)m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n-1}+(n+1)\frac{\|\delta_{ik}\|^{2}}{2}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}c^{\prime}_{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{\ell} \displaystyle\triangleq \displaystyle(n+1)m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n-1}+\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}c^{A}_{\ell}\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{\ell}. $$

Here, we keep the first term explicitly and absorb all the remaining terms into the polynomial in $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|$ , with the resulting constants denoted by $c^{A}_{\ell}>0$ , $\ell=0,\ldots,n-1$ . This establishes the first inequality for $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|\geq 1$ . The second inequality for $f(z-e_{ik})-f(z)$ follows similarly.

Finally, consider $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|<1$ . Since $\|\delta_{ik}\|\leq m_{ik}$ , the increments $f(z\pm e_{ik})-f(z)$ are uniformly bounded, and so are the leading terms $(n+1)m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)\|W_{\perp}(z)\|^{n-1}$ . Thus, by enlarging $c_{0}^{A}$ and $c_{0}^{S}$ if necessary, the same increment bounds hold for $\|W_{\perp}(z)\|<1$ . ∎

### B.2 Proof of Lemma 5.2

#### Proof.

For (5.15), first note from Lemma 3.1 that

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}=1,\text{ and }\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}=1. $$

Moreover, by (4.8),

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{u_{k}}{\mu_{ik}}\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\left(v_{i}+\frac{d_{ik}}{\mu_{ik}}\right)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k} \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{d_{ik}}{\mu_{ik}}\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)\geq 0. $$

Using the definition of $W_{\perp}(z)$ , we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{\perp,k}(z) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}(z) \displaystyle-\frac{1}{\|u\|^{2}}\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}u_{\ell}W_{\ell}(z)\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{u_{k}}{\mu_{ik}}\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}u_{k}\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}(z), $$

where the last inequality follows from the nonnegativity established above and $\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}u_{\ell}W_{\ell}(z)\geq 0$ .

We choose an optimal processing plan $x^{*}$ such that $x^{*}_{ik}>0$ for every basic activity $(i,k)$ . Such a solution exists because, by definition, each basic activity has positive allocation in some optimal processing plan, and a convex combination of these optimal processing plans remains optimal and assigns strictly positive allocation to every basic activity. Define $\lambda_{ik}\triangleq x^{*}_{ik}\mu_{ik}$ for $(i,k)\in\mathcal{J}$ . Then $\lambda_{i}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}$ for each $i\in\mathcal{I}$ and $\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\lambda_{ik}m_{ik}=1$ for each $k\in\mathcal{K}$ . Hence,

$$ \sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}(k)}\lambda_{ik}m_{ik}W_{k}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}m_{ik}W_{k}(z). $$

Moreover, by the definition of the WWTA policy,

$$ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}(z)\big)=\min_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{k}(z). $$

Therefore, using $\lambda_{i}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}$ , the last line of (B.40) can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik^{\prime}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-\sum_{k=1}^{K}W_{k}(z) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}\left[\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik^{\prime}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\right]. $$

For activities with $d_{ik}>0$ , complementary slackness gives $x^{*}_{ik}=0$ and hence $\lambda_{ik}=0$ . We therefore obtain

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\lambda_{ik}\left(\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik^{\prime}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-m_{ik}W_{k}(z)\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\lambda_{ik}v_{i}\left(\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{\mu_{ik^{\prime}}v_{i}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-\frac{1}{\mu_{ik}v_{i}}W_{k}(z)\right) \displaystyle= \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\lambda_{ik}v_{i}\left(\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime}}-d_{ik^{\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)\right). $$

Note that the minimization over $k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)$ is over both basic and non-basic activities, as the WWTA policy does not distinguish between them when making routing decisions. Restricting the minimization to activities with $d_{ik}=0$ can only increase the minimum, and hence

$$ \min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime}}-d_{ik^{\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)\leq\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z), $$

where the superscript “b” indicates restriction to activities with $d_{ik}=0$ . Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\lambda_{ik}v_{i}\left(\min_{k^{\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime}}-d_{ik^{\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime}}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\lambda_{ik}v_{i}\left(\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)\right) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle-\min_{(i,k):\,\lambda_{ik}>0}(\lambda_{ik}v_{i})\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i):\lambda_{ik}>0}\left|\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right|. $$

We next relate the bound in (B.41) to $T_{(K)}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)$ . By Assumption 3.2, all servers communicate. Hence, there exists a path of basic activities connecting the servers attaining $T_{(1)}(z)$ and $T_{(K)}(z)$ . We choose such a path with the fewest servers, so that the job classes along the path are distinct, and hence so are the activities along the path. Moreover, by the choice of $x^{*}$ , all these activities satisfy $\lambda_{ik}>0$ , so their terms appear in the last line of (B.41). To illustrate the argument, consider an example path of the form

$$ (1)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{1}}}{{\rightarrow}}k_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{2}}}{{\rightarrow}}k_{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{3}}}{{\rightarrow}}k_{3}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{4}}}{{\rightarrow}}(K), $$

where each pair of consecutive servers is connected through the indicated job class by basic activities. Retaining only the terms corresponding to this path in the last line of (B.41) and upper bounding all remaining terms by zero, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i):\lambda_{ik}>0}\left|\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i)}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle-\left|T_{(1)}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{1})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right|-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{1}}}W_{k_{1}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{1})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right| \displaystyle-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{1}}}W_{k_{1}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{2})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right|-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{2}}}W_{k_{2}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{2})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right| \displaystyle-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{2}}}W_{k_{2}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{3})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right|-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{3}}}W_{k_{3}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{3})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right| \displaystyle-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{3}}}W_{k_{3}}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{4})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right|-\left|T_{(K)}(z)-\min_{k^{\prime\prime}\in\mathcal{K}(i_{4})}^{b}\frac{1}{u_{k^{\prime\prime}}}W_{k^{\prime\prime}}(z)\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{1}}}W_{k_{1}}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)\right|-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{1}}}W_{k_{1}}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k_{2}}}W_{k_{2}}(z)\right| \displaystyle-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{2}}}W_{k_{2}}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k_{3}}}W_{k_{3}}(z)\right|-\left|\frac{1}{u_{k_{3}}}W_{k_{3}}(z)-T_{(K)}(z)\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle-\left(T_{(K)}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)\right), $$

where the first inequality follows by retaining only the non-positive terms associated with the selected path. The second inequality follows by applying the triangle inequality to each pair of consecutive servers along the path, and the last inequality follows by applying the triangle inequality again along the entire path from $T_{(1)}(z)$ to $T_{(K)}(z)$ . This proves (5.15).

For (5.16), using the definition of $W_{\perp,k}(z)$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle-r\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}m_{ik}W_{\perp,k}(z)\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}({z})\big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle r\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{u_{k}}{u_{k}-d_{ik}}\left[\frac{1}{\|u\|^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}u_{\ell}W_{\ell}(z)-\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)\right]\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}({z})\big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle r\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\frac{u_{k}}{u_{k}-d_{ik}}\left[T_{(K)}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)\right]\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}({z})\big) \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle r\max_{(i,k)}\frac{u_{k}}{u_{k}-d_{ik}}\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\left[T_{(K)}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)\right]\mathbbm{1}\big(k=L^{(i)}({z})\big) \displaystyle= \displaystyle r\max_{(i,k)}\frac{u_{k}}{u_{k}-d_{ik}}\big[T_{(K)}(z)-T_{(1)}(z)\big]. $$

The first inequality follows since both $\frac{1}{\|u\|^{2}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{K}u_{\ell}W_{\ell}(z)$ and $\frac{1}{u_{k}}W_{k}(z)$ lie between $T_{(1)}(z)$ and $T_{(K)}(z)$ . The second inequality follows by taking the maximum of $\frac{u_{k}}{u_{k}-d_{ik}}$ , and the last equality follows from $\sum_{i=1}^{I}\lambda_{i}v_{i}=1$ . This proves (5.16). ∎

where $(i)$ follows from the bounded convergence theorem, since the integrand is bounded for $\theta\leq 0$ , and $(iii)$ follows directly from $(\ref{eq:helper})$ . To justify $(ii)$ , we state the Moore–Osgood theorem in Graves (1946) as follows:

#### Theorem D.1 (Moore–Osgood).

If $\lim_{x\rightarrow p}f(x,y)$ exists pointwise for each $y$ different from $q$ and if $\lim_{y\rightarrow q}f(x,y)$ converges uniformly for $x\neq p$ , then the double limit and the iterated limits exist and are equal, i.e.,

$$ \lim_{(x,y)\rightarrow(p,q)}f(x,y)=\lim_{x\rightarrow p}\lim_{y\rightarrow q}f(x,y)=\lim_{y\rightarrow q}\lim_{x\rightarrow p}f(x,y). $$

To apply the theorem, for each $i\in\mathcal{I}$ , define

$$ \displaystyle g_{i}(r,t)\triangleq \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\bigg[\bigg(\lambda_{i}v_{i}-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}u_{k}P_{ik}({Z}^{(r)})\bigg)e^{r\theta\left(t\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}\right)}f_{\theta}(Z^{(r)})\bigg]. $$

We apply the theorem on the domain $r\in(0,r_{0})$ and $t>0$ and verify its two conditions. First, by $(\ref{eq:helper})$ , $\lim_{r\downarrow 0}g_{i}(r,t)$ exists pointwise for each $t>0$ . To verify the second condition, we use the following lemma, proved in Appendix D.3.

#### Lemma D.1.

For each $i\in\mathcal{I}$ , $\lim_{t\downarrow 0}g_{i}(r,t)$ converges uniformly for $r\in(0,r_{0})$ .

The conditions of the Moore–Osgood theorem are therefore satisfied, so the limits can be interchanged, completing the proof of $(ii)$ .

∎

### D.3 Proof of Lemma D.1

#### Proof.

To prove uniform convergence, it suffices to bound, for $i\in\mathcal{I}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle|g_{i}(r,t)-g_{i}(r,0)| \displaystyle= \displaystyle\left|\mathbb{E}\left[\bigg(\lambda_{i}v_{i}-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}u_{k}P_{ik}({Z}^{(r)})\bigg)e^{r\theta\left(\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}\right)}\left(e^{r\theta t\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}}-1\right)\right]\right| \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\left|\lambda_{i}v_{i}-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}u_{k}P_{ik}({Z}^{(r)})\right|\left|e^{r\theta\left(\sum_{i=1}^{I}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}\right)}\right|\left|e^{r\theta t\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}}-1\right|\right] \displaystyle\leq \displaystyle 2\mathbb{E}\left|\left(e^{r\theta t\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}Z^{(r)}_{ik}}-1\right)\right| \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\leq}} \displaystyle 2|\theta|tr\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}v_{i}\mathbb{E}\left(Z^{(r)}_{ik}\right) \displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\leq}} \displaystyle 2|\theta|v_{i}tM_{0}, $$

where $(a)$ follows from the inequality $1-e^{-x}\leq x$ for $x\geq 0$ , and $(b)$ follows from Lemma 6.3, which ensures that there exists $M_{0}>0$ such that $r\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}(i)}\mathbb{E}\left(Z^{(r)}_{ik}\right)\leq M_{0}$ for all $r\in(0,r_{0})$ . If $\theta=0$ , the result is immediate. For $\theta<0$ and any $\xi>0$ , let

$$ \delta_{i}=\frac{\xi}{3v_{i}M_{0}|\theta|}. $$

Then, for all $r\in(0,r_{0})$ and $0<t<\delta_{i}$ ,

$$ |g_{i}(r,t)-g_{i}(r,0)|\leq 2v_{i}M_{0}|\theta|\frac{\xi}{3v_{i}M_{0}|\theta|}<\xi. $$

Therefore, for each $i\in\mathcal{I}$ , $\lim_{t\downarrow 0}g_{i}(r,t)$ converges uniformly for all $r\in(0,r_{0})$ . ∎

# Adaptive Estimation in Multivariate Response Regression with Hidden Variables

**Authors:** Xin Bing?? Yang Ning Yaosheng Xu

## Abstract

A prominent concern of scientific investigators is the presence of unobserved hidden variables in association analysis. Ignoring hidden variables often yields biased statistical results and misleading scientific conclusions. Motivated by this practical issue, this paper studies the multivariate response regression with hidden variables, $Y=(\Psi^{*})^{T}X+(B^{*})^{T}Z+E$ , where $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the response vector, $X\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is the observable feature, $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ represents the vector of unobserved hidden variables, possibly correlated with $X$ , and $E$ is an independent error. The number of hidden variables $K$ is unknown and both $m$ and $p$ are allowed, but not required, to grow with the sample size $n$ .

Though $\Psi^{*}$ is shown to be non-identifiable due to the presence of hidden variables, we propose to identify the projection of $\Psi^{*}$ onto the orthogonal complement of the row space of $B^{*}$ , denoted by $\Theta^{*}$ . The quantity $(\Theta^{*})^{T}X$ measures the effect of $X$ on $Y$ that cannot be explained through the hidden variables, and thus $\Theta^{*}$ is treated as the parameter of interest. Motivated by the identifiability proof, we propose a novel estimation algorithm for $\Theta^{*}$ , called HIVE, under homoscedastic errors. The first step of the algorithm estimates the best linear prediction of $Y$ given $X$ , in which the unknown coefficient matrix exhibits an additive decomposition of $\Psi^{*}$ and a dense matrix due to the correlation between $X$ and $Z$ . Under the sparsity assumption on $\Psi^{*}$ , we propose to minimize a penalized least squares loss by regularizing $\Psi^{*}$ and the dense matrix via group-lasso and multivariate ridge, respectively. Non-asymptotic deviation bounds of the in-sample prediction error are established. Our second step estimates the row space of $B^{*}$ by leveraging the covariance structure of the residual vector from the first step. In the last step, we estimate $\Theta^{*}$ via projecting $Y$ onto the orthogonal complement of the estimated row space of $B^{*}$ to remove the effect of hidden variables. Non-asymptotic error bounds of our final estimator of $\Theta^{*}$ , which are valid for any $m,p,K$ and $n$ , are established. We further show that, under mild assumptions, the rate of our estimator matches the best possible rate with known $B^{*}$ and is adaptive to the unknown sparsity of $\Theta^{*}$ induced by the sparsity of $\Psi^{*}$ . The model identifiability, estimation algorithm and statistical guarantees are further extended to the setting with heteroscedastic errors. Thorough numerical simulations and two real data examples are provided to back up our theoretical results.

## 1 Introduction

Multivariate response regression has been widely used to evaluate how predictors are associated with multiple response variables and is ubiquitous in many areas including genomics, epidemiology, social science and economics [3]. Most of the existing research on multivariate response regression assumes that the collected predictors are sufficient to explain the responses. However, due to cost constraints or ethical issues, oftentimes there exist unmeasured hidden variables that are associated with the responses as well. Ignoring the hidden variables often leads to biased estimates.

In this paper, we consider the following multivariate response regression with hidden variables. Let $Y\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ denote the response vector, $X\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ denote the observable predictors and $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ be the unobservable hidden variables. The multivariate response regression model postulates

$$ Y=(\Psi^{*})^{T}X+(B^{*})^{T}Z+E, $$

where $\Psi^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}$ and $B^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times m}$ are unknown deterministic matrices and $E\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is a stochastic error with zero mean and a diagonal covariance matrix $\Sigma_{E}$ . The random error $E$ is independent of $(X,Z)$ and the hidden variable $Z$ is possibly correlated with $X$ . The number of hidden variables, $K$ , is unknown and is assumed to be less than $m$ . As we can subtract means from both sides of (1.1), we consider $Y$ , $X$ and $Z$ have mean zero. Without loss of generality, we assume $\Sigma=\text{Cov}(X)$ and $\Sigma_{Z}=\text{Cov}(Z)$ are strictly positive definite and $\textrm{rank}(B^{*})=K$ . Otherwise, one might reduce the dimensions of $X$ and $Z$ such that these conditions are met.

Assume that we observe $n$ i.i.d. copies of $(X,Y)$ and stack them together as a design matrix ${\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and a response matrix ${\bm{Y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ . In practice, the number of response variables $m$ , or the number of features $p$ , or both of them, can be greater than the sample size $n$ .

The proposed model unifies and generalizes the following two strands of research that emerges in a variety of applications.

1. Surrogate variable analysis (SVA) in genomics. The measurements of high-throughput genomic data are often confounded by unobserved factors. To remove the influence of unobserved confounders, surrogate variable analysis (SVA) based on model (1.1) has been proposed for the analysis of biological data [44, 45, 54, 23, 31, 35, 53]. In these applications, the response vector $Y$ is often the gene expression or DNA methylation levels at $m$ sites, which is usually much larger than the sample size $n$ . The covariate $X$ is a small set of exposures (e.g., treatment variables), whose dimension $p$ is assumed to be fixed in the theoretical analysis [43, 56, 47]. Since $p$ is small, the existing SVA methods apply the ordinary least squares (OLS) $({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{Y}}$ to estimate the main regression effect and then remove the bias of the OLS estimator, originating from the correlation between $Z$ and $X$ . However, to avoid confounding issues, researchers tend to collect as many features as possible and adjust them in the regression model afterwards. In this case, $p$ can be large and even much larger than $n$ , whence the existing SVA methods are not applicable as the OLS estimator may not exist. Our work extends the scope of the SVA in the sense that a unified estimation procedure and theoretical justification are developed under model (1.1) where both $p$ and $m$ are allowed, but not required, to grow with $n$ . We refer to Section 1.2 for detailed comparisons with existing SVA literature.

2. Structural equation model in causal inference. Model (1.1) can be also framed as linear structural equation models [36]. Suppose the causal structure among $(X,Z,Y)$ is represented by the directed acyclic graph (DAG) in Figure 1. As shown in this graph, both observed variables $X$ and hidden variables $Z$ are the causes of $Y$ , as $(X,Z)$ are the parents of $Y$ . Under the linearity assumption, the causal structure of $(X,Z)\rightarrow Y$ is modeled by equation (1.1). Similarly, the DAG in Figure 1 also implies that $X$ is the cause of $Z$ , which can be further modeled via

$$ Z=D^{T}X+W, $$

where $D\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times K}$ is a deterministic matrix and $W\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ is a random noise, independent of $X$ and $E$ . Since $Z$ is not observable, model (1.1) and (1.2) are viewed as linear structural equation models with hidden variables [26]. Using the terminology in causal mediation analysis, the parameter $\Psi^{*}$ in (1.1) represents the direct causal effect of $X$ on $Y$ . It is worthwhile to note that the proposed framework is more general than linear structural equation models as model (1.2) is not imposed. In particular, we allow an arbitrary dependence structure between $X$ and $Z$ , whereas the linear structural equation model assumes $X$ is a cause of $Z$ with the independence between $X$ and $W$ .

### 1.1 Our contributions

#### Identifiability

Our first contribution is to investigate the identifiability of model (1.1). We show in Proposition 1 of Section 2.1 that $\Psi^{*}$ in model (1.1) is not identifiable. This motivates us to focus on an alternative estimand, the projection of $\Psi^{*}$ onto the orthogonal complement of the row space of $B^{*}$ , which is identifiable and has desirable interpretations in practice.

We start by rewriting model (1.1). Denote by $(A^{*})^{T}X$ the $L_{2}$ projection of $Z$ onto the linear space of $X$ and by $W=Z-(A^{*})^{T}X$ its residual, where

$$ A^{*}=\left\{\mathbb{E}\left[XX^{T}\right]\right\}^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[XZ^{T}\right]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times K}. $$

We emphasize that we do not require model (1.2), or equivalently, the independence between $W$ and $X$ . For this reason, we use a different notation $A^{*}$ rather than $D$ to denote the coefficient of the $L_{2}$ projection. We then decompose the effect of hidden variable $Z$ as $(B^{*})^{T}Z=(A^{*}B^{*})^{T}X+(B^{*})^{T}W.$ Plugging this into (1.1) yields

$$ \displaystyle Y \displaystyle~=~(\Psi^{*}+A^{*}B^{*})^{T}X+(B^{*})^{T}W+E \displaystyle~=~(\underbrace{\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}}_{\Theta^{*}}+\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+\underbrace{A^{*}B^{*}}_{L^{*}})^{T}X+\underbrace{(B^{*})^{T}W+E}_{\varepsilon}, $$

where $P_{B^{*}}=B^{*T}(B^{*}B^{*T})^{-1}B^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}$ is the projection matrix onto the row space of $B^{*}$ , $P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}={\bm{I}}_{m}-P_{B^{*}}$ , $L^{*}=A^{*}B^{*}$ and the residual vector $\varepsilon=(B^{*})^{T}W+E$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon]=0$ and $\text{Cov}(X,\varepsilon)=0$ .

In (1.4), we decompose $\Psi^{*}$ into two components $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}$ and $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}$ . The former, denoted by $\Theta^{*}$ , is the projection of $\Psi^{*}$ onto the orthogonal complement of the row space of $B^{*}$ . Since ${\Theta^{*}}^{T}X$ is orthogonal to ${B^{*}}^{T}Z$ , ${\Theta^{*}}^{T}X$ measures the effect of $X$ on $Y$ in the multivariate response regression (1.1) that cannot be explained through the effect of hidden variables. In the mediation analysis, $\Theta^{*}$ is referred to as the “partial” direct effect of $X$ on $Y$ .

In Propositions 2 and 3 of Section 2.1 we establish the sufficient and necessary conditions for the identifiability of $\Theta^{*}$ when the error $E$ is homoscedastic, that is $\Sigma_{E}=\tau^{2}{\bm{I}}_{m}$ . This covariance structure of the residual vector $\varepsilon$ is crucial to show the results, as detailed in Section 2.1. However, the sufficiency no longer holds in the presence of heteroscedastic error, when $\Sigma_{E}$ is a diagonal matrix with unequal entries. Inspired by [60], we introduce a mild incoherence condition on the right singular vectors of $B^{*}$ to identify the row space of $B^{*}$ , which is an important intermediate step towards identifying $\Theta^{*}$ . We show in Proposition 9 of Section 4 that this incoherence condition guarantees the identifiability of $\Theta^{*}$ in the heteroscedastic case.

Summarizing, the parameter $\Theta^{*}$ is identifiable under both homoscedastic and heteroscedastic errors. We focus on the estimation of $\Theta^{*}$ throughout the paper. In cases where $\Psi^{*}$ is the primary interest, the information in $\Theta^{*}$ is still helpful to infer $\Psi^{*}$ . In particular, our analysis of $\Theta^{*}$ carries over to $\Psi^{*}$ , under $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}\to 0$ as $m=m(n)\to\infty$ , a common condition of $\Psi^{*}$ in the SVA literature [43]. We refer to Section 5.5 for more detailed discussions of using $\Theta^{*}$ to infer $\Psi^{*}$ .

#### Estimation of $\Theta^{*}$

Our second contribution is to propose a new method for estimating $\Theta^{*}$ . In particular, our approach can handle the case when $p>n$ and the OLS commonly used in the SVA literature does not exist. To deal with the high dimensionality of $\Theta^{*}$ , we assume that there exists a small subset of $X$ that are associated with $Y$ in model (1.1). Such a row-wise sparsity assumption on the coefficient matrix has been widely used in multivariate response regression, for instance, [13, 17, 15, 46, 49, 59], just to name a few. While $\Psi^{*}$ is not identifiable, we assume $\Psi^{*}$ lies in the space $\Omega$

$$ \Psi^{*}\in\Omega:=\left\{M\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times m}:\|M\|_{\ell_{0}/\ell_{2}}\leq s_{*}\right\}, $$

where $s_{*}\leq p$ and $\|M\|_{\ell_{0}/\ell_{2}}=\sum_{j=1}^{p}1_{\{\|M_{j\cdot}\|_{2}\neq 0\}}$ is the number of nonzero rows. As a result, (1.5) implies that $\Theta^{*}\in\Omega$ as

$$ \|\Theta^{*}\|_{\ell_{0}/\ell_{2}}=\|\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}\|_{\ell_{0}/\ell_{2}}\leq s_{*}. $$

Our estimation procedure consists of three steps: first estimate the best linear prediction of $Y$ given $X$ ; then estimate the row space of $B^{*}$ and finally estimate $\Theta^{*}$ .

The first step is critical but challenging especially when $p$ is large. In Section 2.2.1, we propose a new optimization-based approach with a combination of the group-lasso penalty [59] and the multivariate ridge penalty. The group-lasso penalty aims to exploit the row-wise sparsity of $\Psi^{*}$ in (1.5), while the multivariate ridge penalty regularizes the additional dense signal $L^{*}$ due to the hidden variables $Z$ (see model (1.4)). The proposed procedure is easy to implement and has almost the same complexity as solving a group-lasso problem. We refer to Section 2.2.1 for detailed discussions of computational and theoretical advantages of our estimator over other competing methods.

Our second step is to estimate the row space of $B^{*}$ or equivalently $P_{B^{*}}$ . When the noise is homoscedastic, we directly apply the principle component analysis (PCA) to the sample covariance matrix of the estimated residuals (see Section 2.2.2). The resulting first $K$ eigenvectors are then used to estimate $P_{B^{*}}$ . However, PCA may lead to biased estimates under heteroscedastic error, especially when $m$ is fixed. To deal with heteroscedasticity, we adapt the HeteroPCA algorithm, originally proposed by [60], to our setting.

In the last step, we project $Y$ onto the orthogonal complement of the estimated row space of $B^{*}$ to remove the effect of hidden variables, and then recover $\Theta^{*}$ by applying group-lasso to the projected $Y$ .

Our entire procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1, called HIVE, representing HIdden Variable adjustment Estimation. Similarly, the algorithm tailored for the heteroscedastic error is referred to as H-HIVE in Algorithm 3. For the convenience of practitioners, we also provide detailed discussions on practical implementations in Section 5, including estimation of the number of hidden variables ( $K$ ), the consequence of overestimating/underestimating $K$ , the choice of tuning parameters, data standardization and practical usage of $\Theta^{*}$ for inferring $\Psi^{*}$ .

#### Statistical guarantees

Our third contribution is to establish theoretical properties of our procedure. In Theorem 4 of Section 4, we derive non-asymptotic deviation bounds of the in-sample prediction error, which are valid for any finite $n$ , $p$ , $m$ and $K$ . The error bounds consist of three components: bias and variance terms from the ridge regularization and an error term from the group-lasso regularization. To understand the advantage of our estimator, we particularize to the orthonormal design and show that our estimator enjoys the optimal rate of the group-lasso when there is no hidden variable (i.e., $L^{*}=0$ in model (1.4)) and it also achieves the optimal rate of the ridge estimator when $\Psi^{*}=0$ . Thus, the rate of our estimator matches the best possible rate even if $L^{*}=0$ or $\Psi^{*}=0$ were known a priori.

We further provide theoretical guarantees for the estimation of $\Theta^{*}$ . Specifically, we establish in Theorem 6 non-asymptotic upper bounds of the estimation error of our estimator $\widetilde{\Theta}$ based on any estimator $\widehat{P}$ of $P_{B^{*}}$ . As expected, the estimation error of $\widetilde{\Theta}$ depends on the accuracy of $\widehat{P}$ for estimating $P_{B^{*}}$ . When $P_{B^{*}}$ can be estimated accurately, our estimator $\widetilde{\Theta}$ achieves the optimal rate in the oracle case with known $B^{*}$ (see the subsequent paragraph of Theorem 6). However, if the estimation error of $P_{B^{*}}$ is relatively large, we can balance this term with the error of the group-lasso to attain a more refined rate via a suitable choice of the regularization parameter. In Theorem 7 of Section 3.2 and Theorem 10 of Section 4, we further establish non-asymptotic error bounds for our proposed estimators of $P_{B^{*}}$ under both homoscedastic and heteroscedastic errors. These results together with Theorem 6 provide the final upper bounds of the estimation error of $\widetilde{\Theta}$ . To deal with heteroscedastic errors, we develop a new robust $\sin\Theta$ theorem in Appendix A to control the perturbation of eigenspaces in the Frobenius norm. This theorem is essential to the proof of Theorem 10 and can be of its own interest.

### 1.2 Related literature

This work is most related to the literature on surrogate variable analysis (SVA) in which the parameter of interest is $\Psi^{*}$ . Though our target $\Theta^{*}=\Psi^{*}P^{\perp}_{B^{*}}$ is different from $\Psi^{*}$ , our analysis of $\Theta^{*}$ is applicable to $\Psi^{*}$ under the condition $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}=0$ (or $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}\rightarrow 0$ ). We thus compare our results under $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}=0$ with the existing SVA literature. For the identifiability of $\Psi^{*}$ , [31, 56] assumed that there exists a known subset $J\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$ such that the $p\times|J|$ submatrix $\Psi^{*}_{J}=0$ . This set $J$ is known as “negative control” in the microarray studies. However, this side information is usually unknown in other settings. Another approach by [56, 47] assumes that each row $\Psi^{*}_{j\cdot}\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is sparse with $\|\Psi^{*}_{j\cdot}\|_{0}\leq(m-a)/2$ for some $a>K$ and any $K\times a$ submatrix of $B^{*}$ is of rank $K$ . This assumption rules out the possibility that $B^{*}$ could be sparse and the resulting sparsity pattern of $\Psi^{*}$ differs from (1.5), considered in this work. [43] assumed the condition $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}\to 0$ as $m\to\infty$ . In contrast, our identifiability result of $\Theta^{*}$ (which is $\Psi^{*}$ under $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}=0$ ) holds for any finite $n,p,m$ and $K$ . To show the estimation consistency, all existing SVA methods require that $m$ grows with $n$ and is typically much larger than $n$ , meanwhile $p$ is fixed and small, whereas our method provides a more general theoretical framework in which both $p$ and $m$ are allowed, but not required, to grow with $n$ .

[24] studied the estimation of Gaussian graphical models with latent variables. In their setting, one can rewrite their estimand as the sum of a low-rank matrix and a sparse matrix (see [37, 19] for other related examples). The regularized maximum likelihood approach is proposed with a combination of the lasso penalty and the nuclear norm penalty. Our problem is related to theirs, because model (1.4) is a regression problem where the coefficient matrix has an additive decomposition of a sparse and a low-rank matrix when $K$ is much smaller than $p$ and $m$ . However, our work differs significantly from this strand of research in the following aspects. First, the parameter of interest is $\Theta^{*}$ , and thus we do not need the identifiability assumptions in [24]. To see this, consider a simple example based on the regression model (1.4) with $p=m$ and $K=1$ . Let $A^{*}=e_{i}$ and $B^{*}=e_{i}^{T}$ , where $e_{i}$ is the $i$ th canonical basis vector of $\mathbb{R}^{p}$ . The identifiability assumption in [24] does not hold, because the low rank matrix $L^{*}=A^{*}B^{*}=e_{i}e_{i}^{T}$ is too sparse and cannot be distinguished from the sparse matrix $\Psi^{*}$ . However, our target $\Theta^{*}\in\{\Psi^{*}({\bm{I}}_{p}-e_{i}e_{i}^{T}):\Psi^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\}$ is still identifiable when the error is homoscedastic. One explanation is that the covariance structure of $\varepsilon=(B^{*})^{T}W+E$ from model (1.4) can assist the identification of $\Theta^{*}$ , whereas this information is ignored if one directly applies the approach in [24]. Second, due to the differences of identifiability, our estimation algorithm (HIVE or H-HIVE) is fundamentally different from their regularized maximum-likelihood approach. In particular, our regularized estimation in the first step of our algorithm combines the group-lasso penalty and the ridge penalty. We provide a technical comparison of the ridge penalty and the nuclear norm penalty in Appendix D.

Recently, [26] applied SVA to estimate the causal effect under the structural equation models with hidden variables. As discussed previously, the structural equation models assume (1.2), which is not needed in our modeling framework. Our model (1.4) is derived without imposing any specific model between $X$ and $Z$ . For instance, we allow the true dependence structure between $X$ and $Z$ to be very complicated and highly nonlinear. The estimation method of [26] is adapted from the SVA literature, and therefore has the same drawback as SVA. In another recent paper, [22] proposed a new spectral deconfounding approach to deal with high-dimensional linear regression with hidden confounding variables. In particular, their model can be written as a perturbed linear regression $Y=X^{T}(\beta+b)+\epsilon$ where $\epsilon\in\mathbb{R}$ is a random noise, $\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is an unknown sparse vector and $b\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ is a small perturbation vector. In order to identify $\beta$ , they assumed that $\|b\|_{2}$ is sufficiently small. Their estimation method generalizes the lava estimator [25]. Unlike this work, we consider a different setting where the response $Y$ is multivariate and, consequently, both our identifiability and estimation procedures (HIVE and H-HIVE) are completely different from theirs. Our theoretical results in Corollary 8 and its subsequent Remark 6 imply that the convergence rate of our estimator benefits substantially from the multivariate nature of the response, which can be viewed as the blessing of dimensionality.

### 1.3 Outline

In Section 2, we study the identifiability and estimation of $\Theta^{*}$ under homoscedastic error. Sufficient and necessary conditions for the identifiability of $\Theta^{*}$ are established in Section 2.1. Section 2.2 contains three steps of our estimation procedure. The estimation of $\Psi^{*}+L^{*}$ in model (1.4) is stated in Section 2.2.1 and the estimation of the row space of $B^{*}$ is discussed in Section 2.2.2. The final step of estimating $\Theta^{*}$ is stated in Section 2.2.3. Section 3.1 is dedicated to the deviation bounds of the in-sample prediction error. The estimation errors of our estimator of $\Theta^{*}$ together with the errors for estimating the row space of $B^{*}$ are given in Section 3.2. The extension to heteroscedastic case is studied in Section 4. In Section 5, we discuss several practical considerations, including the selection of $K$ , the consequence of overestimating and underestimating $K$ , the choice of tuning parameters, data standardization and practical usage of $\Theta^{*}$ for inferring $\Psi^{*}$ . Simulation results and real data applications are presented in Sections 6 and 7. All proofs and supplementary simulation results are deferred to Supplementary Material.

### 1.4 Notation

For any set $S$ , we write $|S|$ for its cardinality. For any vector $v\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ and some real number $q\geq 0$ , we define its $\ell_{q}$ norm as $\|v\|_{q}=(\sum_{j=1}^{d}|v_{j}|^{q})^{1/q}$ . For any matrix $M\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}$ , $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d_{1}\}$ and $J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d_{2}\}$ , we write $M_{IJ}$ as the $|I|\times|J|$ submatrix of $M$ with row and column indices corresponding to $I$ and $J$ , respectively. In particular, $M_{I\cdot}$ denotes the $|I|\times d_{2}$ submatrix and $M_{J}$ denotes the $d_{1}\times|J|$ submatrix. Further write $\|M\|_{\ell_{p}/\ell_{q}}=(\sum_{j=1}^{d_{1}}\|M_{j\cdot}\|_{\ell_{q}}^{p})^{1/p}$ and denote by $\|M\|_{\ell_{0}}$ , $\|M\|_{op}$ , $\|M\|_{F}$ and $\|M\|_{\infty}$ , respectively, the element-wise $\ell_{0}$ norm, the operator norm, the Frobenius norm and the element-wise sup-norm of $M$ . For any symmetric matrix $M$ , we write $\lambda_{k}(M)$ for its $k$ th largest eigenvalue. For any two sequences $a_{n}$ and $b_{n}$ , we write $a_{n}\lesssim b_{n}$ if there exists some positive constant $C$ such that $a_{n}\leq Cb_{n}$ . Both $a_{n}\asymp b_{n}$ and $a_{n}=\Omega(b_{n})$ stand for $a_{n}=O(b_{n})$ and $b_{n}=O(a_{n})$ . Denote $a\vee b=\max(a,b)$ and $a\wedge b=\min(a,b)$ . Throughout the paper, we will write $\widehat{\Sigma}=n^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}}$ with non-zero eigenvalues $\sigma_{1}\geq\sigma_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_{q}$ and $q:=\textrm{rank}({\bm{X}})$ .

## 2 Identifiability and estimation under homoscedastic noise

As seen in the Introduction, $\Psi^{*}$ is not identifiable under model (1.1) due to the presence of hidden variables. The following proposition formally shows this.

#### Proposition 1.

Under model (1.1), or equivalently (1.4), if $Z\in\mathbb{R}^{K}$ has continuous support and $A^{*}\neq 0$ , then $\Psi^{*}$ is not identifiable.

Despite of the non-identifiability of $\Psi^{*}$ , we proceed to show that $\Theta^{*}=\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}$ is identifiable when the error $E$ is homoscedastic. Our identifiability procedure is constructive and leads to a computationally efficient estimation algorithm for $\Theta^{*}$ .

### 2.1 Identifiability of $\Theta^{*}$

We start by describing our procedure of identifying $\Theta^{*}$ from model (1.4) in three steps:

- (1) identify the coefficient matrix

$$ F^{*}:=\Psi^{*}+A^{*}B^{*}=\Psi^{*}+L^{*}; $$

- (2) identify $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}:=\text{Cov}(\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon=(B^{*})^{T}W+E$ and use it to construct $P_{B^{*}}$ , the projection matrix onto the row space of $B^{*}$ ;

- (3) identify $\Theta^{*}$ from $({\bm{I}}_{m}-P_{B^{*}})Y$ .

Recall that $W=Z-(A^{*})^{T}X$ is independent of $E$ with $A^{*}$ defined in (1.3). In step (2), a key observation from model (1.4) is that, under homoscedastic error, the covariance matrix of $\varepsilon=(B^{*})^{T}W+E$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\Sigma_{\varepsilon}=(B^{*})^{T}\Sigma_{W}B^{*}+\Sigma_{E}=(B^{*})^{T}\Sigma_{W}B^{*}+\tau^{2}{\bm{I}}_{m}, $$

where $\Sigma_{W}=\text{Cov}(W)$ . Recall that $\textrm{rank}(B^{*})=K<m$ . Provided that $\Sigma_{W}$ has full rank, (2.1) implies that the row space of $B^{*}$ coincides with the space spanned by the eigenvectors of $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ corresponding to its largest $K$ eigenvalues. We thus propose to identify $P_{B^{*}}$ via the eigenspace of $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ . Step (3) uses

$$ \displaystyle P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}Y \displaystyle~=~(\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp})^{T}X+(B^{*}P_{B^{*}}^{\perp})^{T}Z+P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}E \displaystyle~=~(\Theta^{*})^{T}X+P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}E, $$

where $P^{\perp}_{B^{*}}={\bm{I}}_{m}-P_{B^{*}}$ . The above identity further implies

$$ \Theta^{*}=\bigl[\text{Cov}(X)\bigr]^{-1}\text{Cov}\left(X,P_{B^{*}}^{\perp}Y\right). $$

The identifiability of $\Theta^{*}$ under the homoscedastic error is summarized in the following proposition.

#### Proposition 2.

Under model (1.4), $\Theta^{*}$ is identifiable if either of the following holds:

- (1) $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+A^{*}B^{*}=0$ ;

- (2) $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ and $\Sigma_{E}=\tau^{2}{\bm{I}}_{m}$ .

Case (1) implies that $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}$ , the direct effect of $X$ on $Y$ explained by $Z$ , can be exactly offset by the indirect effect $A^{*}B^{*}$ . In this case, $\Theta^{*}$ can be recovered directly by regressing $Y$ onto $X$ . Since this is rarely the case in practice, we will focus on $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+A^{*}B^{*}\neq 0$ . Case (2) requires $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ in addition to $\Sigma_{E}=\tau^{2}{\bm{I}}_{m}$ . We show, in Proposition 3 below, that $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ is also necessary for identifying $\Theta^{*}$ if $\mathbb{E}[W|X]=0$ and $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+A^{*}B^{*}\neq 0$ .

#### Proposition 3.

Under model (1.4) with $\mathbb{E}[W|X]=0$ , assume $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+A^{*}B^{*}\neq 0$ . If $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})<K$ , then $\Theta^{*}$ is not identifiable.

Combining Propositions 2 and 3 concludes that, under homoscedastic error, $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}+A^{*}B^{*}\neq 0$ and $\mathbb{E}[W|X]=0$ , $\Theta^{*}$ is identifiable if and only if $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ . The condition $\mathbb{E}[W|X]=0$ is satisfied in many interesting scenarios, such as the structured equation model (1.2) and the multivariate Gaussian model for $(Z,X)$ . In practice, recalling that $W=Z-A^{*T}X$ , $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ is a reasonable assumption as the hidden variable $Z$ usually contains information that cannot be perfectly explained by a linear combination of the observable feature $X$ . Therefore, throughout the paper, we assume $\textrm{rank}(\Sigma_{W})=K$ .

#### Remark 1.

In the SVA literature, [43] assumed $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}\to 0$ as $m=m(n)\to\infty$ . Under this condition, we obtain $\Theta^{*}\approx\Psi^{*}$ for sufficiently large $m$ . In this case, Propositions 2 and 3 provide sufficient and necessary conditions for the identifiability of $\Psi^{*}$ for $m$ large enough. Therefore, our analysis provides complete identifiability results for SVA and it further generalizes to the setting that $\Psi^{*}P_{B^{*}}\not\to 0$ .

#### Remark 2.

Our identifiability results are established when the rows of $\bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ are viewed as i.i.d. realizations of a random vector $X\in\mathbb{R}^{p}$ . When ${\bm{X}}$ is treated as a fixed design matrix, Proposition 1 in [47] provides sufficient conditions on $\Psi^{*}$ and other quantities (such as the sparsity of rows of $\Psi^{*}$ and the magnitude of $B^{*}$ ) under which $\Psi^{*}$ becomes identifiable for sufficiently large $n$ .

### 2.2 Estimation of $\Theta^{*}$

Given the data matrices ${\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and ${\bm{Y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ , our estimation procedure follows the same steps in the analysis of the model identifiability: (1) first estimate ${\bm{X}}F^{*}$ ; (2) then estimate $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ and $P_{B^{*}}$ ; (3) finally estimate $\Theta^{*}$ .

#### 2.2.1 Estimation of $XF^{*}$

Recall that $F^{*}=\Psi^{*}+L^{*}$ is identifiable, where $L^{*}=A^{*}B^{*}$ is a dense matrix and $\Psi^{*}$ is a row-wise sparse matrix satisfying (1.5). We propose to estimate $F^{*}$ by $\widehat{F}=\widehat{\Psi}+\widehat{L}$ where $\widehat{\Psi}$ and $\widehat{L}$ are obtained by solving the following optimization problem

$$ \displaystyle(\widehat{\Psi},~\widehat{L})=\arg\min_{\Psi,L}{1\over n}\left\|{\bm{Y}}-{\bm{X}}(\Psi+L)\right\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\|\Psi\|_{\ell_{1}/\ell_{2}}+\lambda_{2}\|L\|_{F}^{2} $$

with some tuning parameters $\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\geq 0$ . Our estimator is designed to recover both the sparse matrix $\Psi^{*}$ via the group-lasso regularization [59] and the dense matrix $L^{*}$ via the multivariate ridge regularization. Computationally, solving (2.3) is efficient with almost the same complexity of solving a group-lasso problem. Specifically, we have the following lemma.

#### Lemma 1.

Let $(\widehat{\Psi},\widehat{L})$ be any solution of (2.3), and denote

$$ P_{\lambda_{2}}={\bm{X}}\left({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}}+n\lambda_{2}{\bm{I}}_{p}\right)^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{T},\qquad Q_{\lambda_{2}}={\bm{I}}_{n}-P_{\lambda_{2}} $$

for any $\lambda_{2}\geq 0$ such that $P_{\lambda_{2}}$ exists. Then $\widehat{\Psi}$ is the solution of the following problem

$$ \widehat{\Psi}=\arg\min_{\Psi}{1\over n}\left\|Q_{\lambda_{2}}^{1/2}({\bm{Y}}-{\bm{X}}\Psi)\right\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{1}\|\Psi\|_{\ell_{1}/\ell_{2}}, $$

and $\widehat{L}=({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}}+n\lambda_{2}{\bm{I}}_{p})^{-1}{\bm{X}}^{T}({\bm{Y}}-{\bm{X}}\widehat{\Psi})$ , where $Q_{\lambda_{2}}^{1/2}$ is the principal matrix square root of $Q_{\lambda_{2}}$ . Moreover, we have

$$ {\bm{X}}\widehat{F}={\bm{X}}(\widehat{\Psi}+\widehat{L})=P_{\lambda_{2}}{\bm{Y}}+Q_{\lambda_{2}}{\bm{X}}\widehat{\Psi}. $$

Lemma 1 characterizes the role of the regularization parameters $\lambda_{2}$ and $\lambda_{1}$ . When $\lambda_{2}\to 0$ , we have $P_{\lambda_{2}}\approx{\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}})^{+}{\bm{X}}^{T}$ and $Q_{\lambda_{2}}{\bm{X}}\approx 0$ with $({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}})^{+}$ being the Moore-Penrose inverse of ${\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}}$ . Thus, ${\bm{X}}\widehat{F}\approx{\bm{X}}({\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{X}})^{+}{\bm{X}}^{T}{\bm{Y}}$ and $\widehat{F}$ reduces to the minimum norm ordinary least squares estimator (see, for instance, [18]). On the other hand, when $\lambda_{2}\to\infty$ , we have $Q_{\lambda_{2}}\approx{\bm{I}}_{n}$ and $\widehat{L}\approx 0$ whence $\widehat{F}\approx\widehat{\Psi}$ essentially becomes the group-lasso estimator. Later in Remark 4 of Section 3.1, we will take a closer look at this phenomenon in terms of the convergence rates of $\|{\bm{X}}\widehat{F}-{\bm{X}}F^{*}\|_{F}$ under the orthonormal design. The tuning parameter $\lambda_{1}$ only appears in (2.5) and its magnitude controls the sparsity level of the group-lasso estimator $\widehat{\Psi}$ . Lemma 1 also implies that the estimator $(\widehat{\Psi},\widehat{L})$ is unique if and only if the solution of the group-lasso problem (2.5) is unique. Even if (2.5) has multiple solutions, we can define $(\widehat{\Psi},\widehat{L})$ to be any of the solutions and the resulting best linear predictor ${\bm{X}}\widehat{F}={\bm{X}}(\widehat{\Psi}+\widehat{L})$ satisfies the desired deviation bounds stated in Theorem 4 of Section 3.1.

In applications when both $m$ and $p$ are large while $K$ is small, $L^{*}$ can be also viewed as a low-rank matrix with rank $K$ . One common approach of estimating a low-rank matrix is to either impose a rank constraint on the matrix, known as the reduced-rank approach [40], or regularize its nuclear norm. We emphasize that, under model (1.4), our approach with the ridge penalty has both theoretical and computational advantages over these two methods. We defer to Appendix D for both theoretical and numerical comparisons.

Finally, we comment that our method (2.3) can be viewed as the multivariate generalization of the lava approach proposed by [25]; see also [22]. Lava estimates the sum of a sparse vector $\beta$ and a dense vector $b$ in linear regression problem ${\bm{y}}={\bm{X}}(\beta+b)+{\bm{\epsilon}}$ by minimizing the least squares loss plus the penalty $\lambda_{1}\|\beta\|_{1}+\lambda_{2}\|b\|_{2}^{2}$ . As explained in [25], lava is intrinsically different from the elastic net as lava penalizes both $\beta$ and $b$ and the estimate of $(\beta+b)$ is non-sparse, whereas elastic net uses the penalty $\lambda_{1}\|\beta\|_{1}+\lambda_{2}\|\beta\|_{2}^{2}$ and typically yields a sparse estimate of $\beta$ . These differences naturally extend to our multivariate setting.

#### 2.2.2 Estimation of $P_{B^{*}}$

In this section, we discuss how to estimate the projection matrix $P_{B^{*}}$ . Consider the singular value decomposition $B^{*}=VDU^{T}$ , where $V\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K}$ and $U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times K}$ are, respectively, the left and right singular vectors of $B^{*}$ , and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of non-increasing singular values. It is easily seen that $P_{B^{*}}=UU^{T}$ . Recall that, from (2.1), $U$ also coincides with the first $K$ eigenvectors of $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ up to an orthogonal matrix. We thus propose to first estimate $\Sigma_{\varepsilon}$ by

$$ \widehat{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}={1\over n}\left({\bm{Y}}-{\bm{X}}\widehat{F}\right)^{T}\left({\bm{Y}}-{\bm{X}}\widehat{F}\right), $$

with $\widehat{F}$ obtained from (2.3), and then estimate $P_{B^{*}}$ by $\widehat{P}_{B^{*}}=\widehat{U}\widehat{U}^{T}$ , where $\widehat{U}$ consists of the eigenvectors of $\widehat{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}$ corresponding to the $K$ largest eigenvalues. We assume $K$ is known for now and defer to Section 5.1 for detailed discussions of selecting $K$ .

#### 2.2.3 Estimation of $\Theta^{*}$

After estimating $P_{B^{*}}$ by $\widehat{P}_{B^{*}}$ , motivated by (2.2), we propose to estimate $\Theta^{*}$ by

$$ \widetilde{\Theta}=\arg\min_{\Theta}{1\over n}\left\|{\bm{Y}}\left({\bm{I}}_{m}-\widehat{P}_{B^{*}}\right)-{\bm{X}}\Theta\right\|_{F}^{2}+\lambda_{3}\|\Theta\|_{\ell_{1}/\ell_{2}} $$

with some tuning parameter $\lambda_{3}>0$ . Solving the problem in (2.8) is equivalent to solving a group-lasso problem with the projected response matrix ${\bm{Y}}({\bm{I}}_{m}-\widehat{P}_{B^{*}})$ .

For the reader’s convenience, we summarize our procedure, HIdden Variable adjustment Estimation (HIVE), in Algorithm 1.

*Algorithm 1 The HIVE procedure for estimating $\Theta^{*}$ .*

```
1: Data ${\bm{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}$ and ${\bm{Y}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ , rank $K$ , tuning parameters $\lambda_{1}$ , $\lambda_{2}$ and $\lambda_{3}$ .
2: Estimate ${\bm{X}}\widehat{F}$ with $\widehat{F}=\widehat{\Psi}+\widehat{L}$ by solving (2.3).
3: Obtain $\widehat{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}$ from (2.7).
4: Compute $\widehat{P}_{B^{*}}=\widehat{U}\widehat{U}^{T}$ where $\widehat{U}$ are the first $K$ eigenvectors of $\widehat{\Sigma}_{\varepsilon}$ .
5: Estimate $\Theta^{*}$ by $\widetilde{\Theta}$ obtained from (2.8).
```

## 3 Statistical guarantees

In this section, we provide theoretical guarantees for our estimation procedure. In our theoretical analysis, the design matrix ${\bm{X}}$ is considered to be deterministic and the analysis can be done similarly for random designs by first conditioning on ${\bm{X}}$ . Recall from model (1.4) that $W$ is uncorrelated with $X$ . To simplify the analysis under the fixed design scenario, we assume the independence between $X$ and $W$ in order to derive the deviation bounds of their cross product. We expect that the same theoretical guarantees hold under $\text{Cov}(X,W)=0$ by using more tedious arguments. We start with the following assumptions on the error matrices ${\bm{W}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times K}$ and ${\bm{E}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$ .

#### Assumption 1.

Let $\gamma_{w}$ and $\gamma_{e}$ denote some positive constants.

(1) Assume $\bigl\{\Sigma_{W}^{-1/2}{\bm{W}}_{i\cdot}\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are i.i.d. $\gamma_{w}$ sub-Gaussian random vectors11 1 A random vector $X$ is $\gamma$ sub-Gaussian if $\langle u,X\rangle$ is $\gamma$ sub-Gaussian for any $\|u\|_{2}=1$ ., where $\Sigma_{W}=\text{Cov}({\bm{W}}_{i\cdot})$ .

(2) For any fixed $1\leq j\leq m$ , $\bigl\{{\bm{E}}_{ij}\bigr\}_{i=1}^{n}$ are i.i.d. $\gamma_{e}$ sub-Gaussian22 2 A centered random variable $X$ is $\gamma$ sub-Gaussian if it satisfies $\mathbb{E}[\exp(tX)]\leq\exp(\gamma^{2}t^{2}/2)$ for all $t\geq 0$ .. For any fixed $1\leq i\leq n$ , $\bigl\{{\bm{E}}_{ij}\bigr\}_{j=1}^{m}$ are independent.

Since part $(2)$ of Assumption 1 does not assume ${\bm{E}}_{ij}$ are identically distributed across $1\leq j\leq m$ , this assumption is applicable to both homoscedastic and heteroscedastic errors, provided that $\max_{1\leq j\leq p}\textrm{Var}({\bm{E}}_{ij})\leq\gamma_{e}^{2}$ . We assume $\Sigma_{E}=\text{Cov}(E)=\tau^{2}{\bm{I}}_{m}$ throughout this section and defer the dicussion of the heteroscedastic case to Section 4. Finally, recall from (1.5) that $\|\Psi^{*}\|_{\ell_{0}/\ell_{2}}\leq s_{*}$ .

### 3.1 Statistical guarantees of estimating $XF^{*}$

To establish theoretical properties for ${\bm{X}}\widehat{F}$ obtained from (2.5), we first generalize the design impact factor of ${\bm{X}}$ in [25] to multivariate response regression settings. Denote $\widetilde{\bm{X}}=Q_{\lambda_{2}}^{1/2}{\bm{X}}$ , where $Q_{\lambda_{2}}$ is defined in (2.4). For notational simplicity, we suppress the dependence of $\widetilde{\bm{X}}$ on $\lambda_{2}$ .
